title: The Painter
poem_text:
there was a painter
who once said
that reality is the least honest thing in the world.

everyone laughed at him for that.

because reality is measurable, isn’t it?
touchable. visible.
it exists in definite shapes
and names that stay still long enough
for language to hold them.

but he kept thinking of all the things
that had changed him completely
without ever becoming visible at all.

how do you paint the feeling
of returning home
and realising you no longer belong to it
in quite the same way?

how do you paint the exact moment
someone stops being a person you know
and quietly becomes part
of the architecture of your inner world?

how do you paint longing
before it learns its own name?

he spent years trying.

not painting people…
people were easy.
faces are only geometry.
light resting temporarily on bone.

he wanted to paint the invisible movements beneath them.

the unbearable tenderness
of someone remembering the smallest thing about you.

the strange ache
of watching time pass through another person’s face.

the way grief does not arrive screaming,
but instead slips silently into ordinary objects;
a half-read book,
an untouched cup of coffee,
a chair angled slightly toward the door
as if still waiting.

he painted in impossible colors.

not red,
but the color of almost becoming.

not blue,
but the color of memories
that feel more alive
than the moments themselves ever did.

people looked at his canvases and said,
“this doesn’t look real.”

and he always wanted to ask them…

was the trembling in your chest real
the first time you realized
another human being
had somehow altered the gravity inside you?

is music unreal
because you cannot hold it in your hands?

is a dream less true
simply because morning survives it?

he believed truth lived elsewhere.

not in objects themselves,
but in the silent spaces surrounding them.

in pauses during conversations.
in the unbearable intimacy of being understood accidentally.
in the silence after laughter fades,
when you suddenly become aware
of how temporary every beautiful thing is.

that was what he painted.

not reality itself,
but the wound reality leaves behind
when it touches the soul deeply enough.

and one night,
after years of failure,
he painted something that frightened him.

it was not a person.
not a landscape.
not anything recognizable.
just light
falling through a half open door
into an empty room.

but somehow,
inside that room
lived every goodbye he had never recovered from,
every version of himself
he had abandoned to survive,
every fleeting beautiful thing
he had loved too deeply
to keep.

he stared at the canvas for hours afterward.

because for the first time in years,
he had not painted what something looked like.

he had painted
what it meant to lose it.

and perhaps that is the closest art ever comes
to telling the truth…

not by reproducing the world faithfully,
but by revealing the invisible devastations
required to survive it.

because the truth does not live
in reality itself.

it lives in the place
where reality ends
and feeling begins.
author_intent: I wanted to explore the difference between reproducing what is visible and expressing what an experience actually means. The painter finds truth in the emotional traces that ordinary objects and moments carry, rather than in their outward appearance.

title: These Mountains
poem_text:
these mountains that you are holding,
you were only supposed to climb.

they were never meant for your shoulders,
they were meant for your steps.

for the shaky knees,
the lungs that burn,
the soul that feels lighter each time.

i thought maybe the ache was proof of living—
but no, love,
you weren't born to collapse under the sky.

you were born to touch it.

so set it down.
breathe.
just climb.
author_intent: I wanted to distinguish facing difficulties from carrying them as permanent burdens. Struggling is not the purpose of living; the mountain is something to move through, not something that must define or exhaust us.

title: Forward Is Forward
poem_text:
forward is forward,
even when it feels like nothing changed today.
you are still moving,
still weaving little threads of tomorrow
with every breath you take.

the river doesn’t rush all the time—
sometimes it drifts,
sometimes it rests,
but it always flows.

so do you.

you don’t need to hurry.
you don’t need to prove.
you are enough in your becoming,
enough in your slow and steady light.

rest in that truth:
you are on your way,
and that is more than enough.
author_intent: I wanted to make room for progress that is slow or invisible. Rest and uncertainty do not necessarily mean that we have stopped growing, and our worth does not depend on constantly proving ourselves.

title: Broken Glass
poem_text:
she didn’t just pick up the pieces,
she bled on them,
she carved her pain into them,
and built a mosaic the world had never seen.

the world called her broken,
but they didn’t know—
broken glass reflects more light
than something whole ever could.

she was no longer a girl piecing herself together,
she was the fire that rose from her own ashes.
and when she walked,
the air shifted—
for she carried a new truth:
broken isn’t the end,
broken is the beginning.
author_intent: I wanted to portray recovery as transformation rather than a return to an earlier, undamaged self. The mosaic represents making something new from painful experiences without pretending those experiences never happened.

title: rooms that remember truth
poem_text:
.
there’s a kind of magic in walking slow,
through halls where the light feels older than the walls.
it lands in soft pools
on leather chairs,
dusty book edges,
half-sipped tea.
everything still.
everything listening.
.
the paintings don’t speak—
but they watch.
and in that watching,
you realize:
some things don’t need words
to be understood.
.
there’s a book that’s been waiting for me
for years.
not because it holds answers—
but because it holds
the questions
i’m finally ready to ask.
.
and maybe that’s what depth is.
not something you dig into,
but something you grow beside.
like how silence can be full.
or how a moment can stretch
and still feel complete.
.
in these quiet corners,
i feel like the world stops measuring me.
not by how much i do,
but by how much i notice.
how long i can sit with a thought
without running away.
.
truth doesn’t always knock.
sometimes, it just
waits.
.
and you find it
in a dusty bookstore,
in the gold frame of a stranger’s portrait,
in the way a page turns slowly—
not revealing,
but remembering.
author_intent: I wanted to explore how stillness makes us receptive to beauty, understanding and self-awareness. Sometimes we become ready for a question rather than finding an answer, and noticing can matter more than accomplishing.

title: and the canary kept singing
poem_text:
what if the spear missed?

what if the gods blinked —
just once —
and the little bird slipped through their fingers?

rue lives.

not untouched.
not unharmed.
but changed.

something in her eyes turns glassy,
like she’s seen past the veil
and returned with silence stitched beneath her tongue.

katniss finds her in the hollow of a tree,
blood dried like rust along her arms,
still singing —
a lullaby with no melody,
just breath and tremble and grief.

they move through the arena like ghosts.
not hunted.
haunting.

rue speaks less now.
only in riddles.
only in dreams.

“they built this place on bones,” she whispers,
“so it will starve when we give it none.”

they starve the game.
refuse violence.
refuse story.

they smear mud on the cameras,
string up dolls from branches,
tear the eyes from the trees.

panem watches.
the capitol seethes.

these are not girls.
they are omens.

and when the final order comes —
“one must die” —
they do not flinch.

rue walks to the center.
barefoot.
no weapon.
no tears.

“you want blood?”
her voice cracks like a hymn.
“then choke on mine.”

she opens her arms.
calls down fire.

they call it a system failure.
a broadcast glitch.
a technical tragedy.

but the districts know.

they saw the girl who lived
walk into the flames
with a smile that didn’t belong in this world.

katniss is crowned.
but her eyes are empty.
she dreams of twisted roots,
a songbird without a beak,
and smoke that tastes like rue’s breath.

the games ended.
but something older woke up that day.
and it sings still —
low, cold, and vengeful
in every crack of the stone.
author_intent: I wanted to imagine Rue surviving and changing the rules of the Games through refusal and resistance. Her eventual sacrifice exposes the violence of a system that depends on turning suffering into spectacle.

title: the orchard fed her bones
poem_text:
.
they said the girl died clean.
.
they lied.
.
rue did not die.
rue was taken.
swallowed by the trees,
stitched back together with rot and root,
reassembled in the dark belly of the arena —
a girl reborn, not in grace, but in vengeance.
.
when katniss finds her,
she is not whole.
her eyes are too black,
too still.
her voice, when it comes, sounds like something buried too long.
.
"they tried to harvest me,” she says,
“but the orchard took me first.”
.
.
.
she bleeds sap.
she sings in tongues.
she moves like something that remembers being human
but isn’t anymore.
.
katniss follows her anyway.
of course she does.
even when the air turns sour,
even when the trees whisper names not spoken in decades,
even when the ground breathes beneath their feet.
.
the arena begins to decay.
.
moss spreads like rot across the cornucopia.
cameras crack.
mutts gnaw at their own paws.
the sky weeps black rain.
.
and rue moves through it all, untouched,
a child-shaped plague.
.
the Capitol sends in fire.
.
rue laughs.
it is the sound of teeth on bone.
.
“they want a show?”
her smile is a wound.
“then let them choke on ruin.”
.
.
.
she does not die.
she unravels.
.
at the final countdown, when only two remain,
she walks to the center of the arena
and opens her mouth wide.
.
from her throat pours ash,
carrion birds,
fragments of hymns older than the Capitol itself.
.
the screen goes black.
no victor.
no anthem.
.
just silence.
.
in the weeks that follow,
district children begin waking with soil under their nails.
the woods grow wrong.
mockingjays fall from the sky mid-song.
and in the corners of mirrors,
they see her —
small, barefoot, watching.
.
still humming.
author_intent: I wanted to imagine a darker version of Rue surviving, where the arena transforms her into something that turns its violence against its creators. The horror represents the consequences of exploitation returning to haunt the system.

title: the phoenix knows
poem_text:
the phoenix knows
that burning isn't always violent.
sometimes, it's quiet—
a slow undoing,
a surrender to gravity
before the sky remembers your name.
.
she doesn’t rise for glory.
she rises because there’s nothing left
but the choice
to begin again.
.
ash is not the end.
it is memory—
of what was heavy,
what had to fall apart.
.
and from it,
she gathers herself—
not new,
but changed.
.
not untouched,
but honest.
.
each feather a story
of what the fire took,
and what it couldn’t.
.
the phoenix never asks
to be seen.
she only asks
to survive.
and still,
she rises.
author_intent: I wanted to portray survival as something quieter than a triumphant comeback. The phoenix carries the memory of what happened and rises because beginning again is the only choice left, not because she wants recognition.

title: wax child
poem_text:
i saw her hold him like he was whole —
a mother and son, a stitched-up soul.
they walked through noise,
but she only heard
his laugh,
his little word.

then —
a scream in steel.
a shot, too real.
her leg caught fire
but her voice stayed calm.
she only ached
for her baby’s palm.

he stood so still,
in the heart of it all,
watched her stumble,
watched her fall.
a tear slipped down —
and he began to fade.
his skin ran soft.
his shape unmade.

not a boy.
never one.
just wax beneath a dying sun.
and still,
she reached.
she called his name
like love alone
could stop the flame.

he broke.
limbs cracked,
cold and light.
and she held him close
like it was all right.

they said
“he was never real.”
but what do they know
of the way we feel?

she rocked him slow
with empty hands,
still humming songs
he’d never understand.

and when they pulled
her grief away,
her arms were shaped
for him to stay.
author_intent: I wanted to question whether love and grief become less real when the object of attachment is not conventionally alive. The mother’s attachment remains meaningful even as the child’s physical form disappears.

title: It Starts With Thought
poem_text:
Before the hand can draw a line,
before the stars are made to shine,
before the world can call it mine—
a thought must whisper, soft, divine.

It doesn't shout, it doesn’t show,
it plants its seeds and lets them grow.
What blooms in time, the world will know—
but roots run deep where thoughts first go.

A moment’s pause, a silent spark,
can shift the day, can light the dark.
The smallest drift, the slightest mark—
can leave behind a lasting arc.

So guard your mind, both wild and wide,
for that’s the place where truths decide.
All that you do, and what you hide—
began with thought, not step or stride.
author_intent: I wanted to reflect on the invisible beginnings of creation and action. A thought may seem insignificant, but it can shape choices and eventually leave a lasting effect on the world.

title: The Knowing Quiet
poem_text:
Listen to the wind—it speaks in sighs,
in dancing leaves and open skies.
It tells of things you used to feel,
before the world taught you to kneel.

Listen to the silence—it holds space,
for every tear you didn't face.
It doesn't judge, it doesn't flee,
it simply waits for you to see.

Listen to your heart—it knows the way,
through broken nights and heavy days.
It may be soft, but it is strong—
it hums the truth when all feels wrong.

There is a voice beneath the noise,
beyond the crowds, beyond the choice.
It lives in stillness, breath, and flame—
and when you hear it, you're not the same.
author_intent: I wanted to explore the quieter parts of ourselves that become easier to notice away from external noise and expectations. Silence can make room for emotion and self-understanding.

title: Call of the Brave
poem_text:
There was never a promise of safety,
only the whisper of stars beyond sight—
a voice in the wind that said go,
that dared the heart to ignite.

The path was not paved with answers,
nor lit by lanterns of ease;
it twisted through thunder and silence,
through forests that brought you to knees.

But those who walked it with wonder,
with fire in marrow and bone,
found treasures not made of silver—
but courage, carved deep in their own.

So cast off the cloak of comfort,
step past the walls of known.
For life is not meant to be measured—
but tasted, and risked, and grown.
author_intent: I wanted to portray courage as moving beyond certainty rather than being guaranteed safety. The value of an unfamiliar journey lies partly in how it changes us, rather than in what we acquire.
